claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes single-phase solid solutions in bulk high-entropy alloys.
Suppressing intermetallic-forming Fe- and Mn-containing combinations is critical to the intrinsic stability of five-transition-metal HENA.
Al-Ti is an intermetallic-forming pair whose presence threatens HENA stability.
The absence of phonon-mediated lattice-softening modes is critical to the intrinsic high-temperature stability of HENA.
Violation of the proposed chemical and phonon constraints will cause rapid phase decomposition in HENA.
Violation of the proposed constraints will cause Ostwald ripening in HENA.
HENA will decompose at temperatures significantly below predictions from standard CALPHAD models that omit phonons and nanoparticle surface energy.
Mechanical alloying or spark plasma sintering can produce nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal nanoparticles with a single FCC or BCC solid-solution phase.
Nanoparticle surface energy governs structural evolution during elevated-temperature exposure.
L2_1 or Heusler-phase formation is governed by atomic occupancy rules sensitive to local chemistry and phonon modes.
Reduced dimensionality amplifies specific chemical interactions and phonon effects relative to bulk alloys.
Current theoretical treatments of high-entropy-alloy phase transitions can omit explicit phonon effects.
Omitting phonon effects from thermodynamic models systematically overestimates phase stability.
Silicides, B2 phases, and Laves phases that form in refractory HEAs can be intrinsically brittle.
HENA containing intermetallic-prone pairs will undergo rapid phase separation and grain growth at temperatures where corresponding bulk alloys remain stable.
Avoiding intermetallic-prone pairs will enhance HENA thermal stability until phonon-driven lattice softening begins.
The NbTaTiV refractory HEA retains a single BCC phase up to 900°C.
W-Ta-V-Cr maintains single-phase stability up to 900°C because of high entropy of mixing and sluggish diffusion.
Current thermodynamic databases can inaccurately describe L2_1-phase stability in Al-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ti high-entropy alloys.
For nanoparticles with negligible intermetallic-forming tendencies, surface-energy stabilization could produce stability comparable to or greater than that of bulk alloys.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis makes stability depend on both intermetallic-forming pairs and phonon softening, yet decomposition of Set B below 600°C is declared falsifying solely because intermetallic-prone pairs are absent. Such decomposition could instead be consistent with the proposed phonon or surface-energy mechanisms.

The design specifies isothermal annealing at 700°C, but the falsification rule requires determining whether decomposition occurs below 600°C and comparing decomposition temperatures. A single 700°C exposure does not by itself establish either threshold.
